name: Roman Empire
era: 27 BCE to 476 CE in the West
line: Do your duty in the morning, bathe in the afternoon and dine with friends.

quote.text: We are not born for ourselves alone.
quote.source: On Duties 1.22, written in 44 BCE; he is citing Plato. Translated from the Latin

quotes.text: The Roman state stands on its ancient customs and its men.
quotes.source: Annals, 2nd century BCE, as quoted by Cicero in On the Republic 5.1. Translated from the Latin

quotes.text: Remember, Roman, that it is for you to rule the nations with your power: to crown peace with law, to spare the conquered and to war down the proud.
quotes.source: Aeneid 6.851 to 853, about 19 BCE. Translated from the Latin

quotes.text: They make a desert and call it peace.
quotes.source: Agricola 30, about 98 CE. Words he gives to the Caledonian chief Calgacus before battle

quotes.text: Captive Greece took her fierce conqueror captive.
I found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble.
quotes.source: As reported by Suetonius, Life of Augustus 28

quotes.text: You should pray for a sound mind in a sound body.

words.usage: Doing what you owe to gods, parents, family and country. The quality of Aeneas, who carried his father out of burning Troy on his back.
A settled, responsible bearing. A Roman of standing did not hurry, chatter or lose his temper in public.
Keeping your word. It had a temple on the Capitol, and treaties were kept there.
From vir, a man. First bravery in battle, then every kind of public merit.
The rank and respect earned by service. Caesar said it was dearer to him than life.
The power to be listened to without giving orders. Augustus claimed to exceed everyone in this and no one in formal power.
Unwritten custom. The first argument in any Roman dispute was that the forefathers had done it so.
The commonwealth that belongs to the people. The emperors kept the word and the forms.
Civis Romanus sum, I am a Roman citizen, was a claim to legal protection anywhere in the empire.
The right to give orders, held by a magistrate. Later the territory over which Rome gave them.
Two centuries of comparative internal peace from Augustus onward, kept by thirty legions on the frontiers.
Literally not-leisure. The public and private duties of the morning.
Free time, ideally spent on reading, writing, friends and one’s estate. Leisure with dignity was the goal of a career.
What you owe to those you are tied to: attending a friend’s ceremony, witnessing a will, speaking in a case.
Everyone under one head: wife, children, freed people and slaves. Wider than our word family.
The oldest living male in the line, who held legal power over all the rest.
A man of means who protects and helps those below him, and expects their loyalty and attendance.
One who has put himself under a patron. The whole of society was a ladder of such ties.
At first light clients called on their patron at home to pay respects and receive help or a small gift.
Market, law court, meeting place and stage of politics. Every Roman town had one.
Vast heated complexes with pools, exercise yards, gardens and libraries, open to all for a small coin or nothing.
The main meal, taken in the late afternoon after the bath, reclining, in company.
Shown as two dancing youths pouring wine. Every home had a shrine to them.
A niche or small painted temple in the house where the family made its daily offering.

words.meaning: The guardian spirit of a person or place
words.usage: Every man had one, honoured on his birthday. Women had a Juno.
A heavy half-circle of white wool, worn draped. Awkward and hot, and required for all public business.
A house looking inward on an open hall and a garden court. Most city people lived in flats instead.
Literally an island. Blocks of five or six storeys, with shops below and the poorest at the top.
Education joined to kindness. Cicero’s word for what makes a person civilised.
Chariot races, plays and fights given free on festival days by magistrates and emperors.

practices.name: At the household shrine
practices.instructions: Choose a shelf or niche in your home and make it the place of the house. Put there something from your family’s past and a small lamp or candle. Each morning at first light, stand before it. Light the lamp. Set down a small offering of bread, a flower or a few drops of olive oil. Say thank you for the house. The rule of this Onda is to honour your household first.
practices.why: Every Roman house had a lararium for the household spirits, the Lares, honoured daily. A shelf of family things and a candle is the modern version.
variations: Add a photograph of an ancestor.
Light the lamp at dusk as well.

practices.name: Duty before noon
practices.instructions: Give the first hours of the day to what you owe other people. Start with two calls. Greet someone who has helped you, a patron, teacher or elder, and ask if there is anything you can do. Then make yourself available to someone who depends on you. Answer the requests that are yours. Business in the morning, leisure after. The rule of this Onda is to do business first.
practices.why: A Roman day began with negotium, business, and the morning greeting, salutatio, of clients to their patrons. The idea of putting duty first and leisure after is a good rhythm.
variations: Make a list of what you owe.
Close the morning with a nod to those you served.

practices.name: Greet an elder
practices.instructions: Pay a morning visit or phone call to an older person or a mentor, as a Roman client called on a patron at dawn. Greet them with respect, ask after their health and offer help. Listen to their advice. Fides, good faith, meant keeping up such ties. Thank them and mean it.
practices.why: The salutatio was a daily ritual of paying respects. Keeping up relationships with older or wiser people is a wise habit in any age.
variations: Write a note to a mentor.

practices.name: Bear yourself with weight
practices.instructions: Stand tall before the day starts. Put on something that feels dignified, a good coat, a scarf draped like a toga, a pin. Walk slowly and steadily, with a straight back, for your first ten steps. Gravitas, weight, was a Roman virtue: a settled seriousness, not stiffness. Carry it lightly, and relax when the day gets going.
practices.why: Gravitas was the Roman virtue of dignity and seriousness. A little posture practice goes a long way.

practices.name: A Latin phrase a day
practices.instructions: Learn one Latin phrase today and use it three times: carpe diem, festina lente, per aspera ad astra, veni vidi vici, in vino veritas, tempus fugit. Say it aloud and write it on your hand. Latin is still alive in law, medicine, science and mottoes. Learning a phrase a day builds a surprising stock.
practices.why: Latin has left thousands of phrases in everyday English. Learning one a day connects you to Rome in a small, fun way.
variations: Learn a motto of your town.
Learn a phrase from a gravestone.

practices.name: A Roman breakfast
practices.instructions: Eat a quick Roman ientaculum: bread dipped in a little wine and water (or in juice), with cheese, olives, figs or honey. Eat it standing or sitting briefly, without ceremony. Romans ate a light breakfast and the main meal in the evening. Notice how a simple breakfast leaves room for the day.
practices.why: Roman breakfasts were small and quick, bread with cheese and fruit. The simple habit is both pleasant and practical.
variations: Dip your bread in olive oil.

practices.name: The baths
practices.instructions: In mid-afternoon stop work and look after the body. First exercise until you are warm and lightly sweating: ball games, running, weights, wrestling. Then bathe in the Roman order. A warm room or warm water to open the skin, a hot soak or shower, then a cool rinse to close. Rest with a cloth around you. Do not stay in heat if you feel faint, and drink water. The rule of this Onda is to bathe and exercise every day.
practices.why: The Roman baths were the centre of daily life for rich and poor, a mix of gym, spa, library and club. An hour spent in the same order brings a bit of that rhythm.
variations: Visit a public pool or sauna.
Do the exercise with a friend.

practices.name: A ball in the afternoon
practices.instructions: Play ball with someone for twenty minutes: catch and throw, kick, a passing game in a park. Romans played several ball games before bathing: harpastum, a rough scramble, and a gentler game with a small ball. Toss it back and forth, count catches and laugh. Play gently and stay safe.
practices.why: Ball games were a favourite exercise before the baths. The poet Martial and the emperor Augustus both played.
variations: Play a gentle game in a pair.

practices.name: Keep faith
practices.instructions: Keep one promise today to the letter, even if it is awkward or inconvenient. Be on time, pay what you owe, return what you borrowed. Fides, good faith, was the Roman virtue that held trade and law together. Say aloud: my word is my bond. The rule of this Onda is to keep faith.
practices.why: Fides, trustworthiness, was worshipped as a goddess in Rome and was the glue of agreements. Keeping faith on small matters builds a reputation.
variations: Return a borrowed item with a thank you.

practices.name: A stroll in the forum
practices.instructions: Take a slow stroll through the busiest public space near you: a market square, a high street, a plaza. Look at everything. Greet a few people. Stop for a conversation. The forum was the heart of a Roman town, where business, law, religion and gossip all met. Spend half an hour as a citizen among citizens.
practices.why: The Roman forum was a town’s meeting place. A stroll among people is a good antidote to a day alone at a screen.
variations: Stop at a stall and chat.
Sit on a bench and watch.
Pick up a newspaper and read it aloud.

practices.name: Write some graffiti
practices.instructions: On a scrap of paper, write a short piece of Pompeii-style graffiti: a joke, a greeting, a boast or a verse. The walls of Pompeii are scratched with lines like Gaius was here, and Whoever loves, let him flourish. Make yours witty. Pin it up for a day or read it to a friend. Do not write on anything that is not yours.
practices.why: The graffiti of Pompeii give a lively view of daily Roman life: love, insults, shopping lists. Writing your own on paper is harmless fun.

practices.name: Go to market
practices.instructions: Go to a market or shop and buy fresh food for the evening meal, as a Roman would, from the stalls. Chat with the sellers, ask what is good today and choose by smell and look. Carry it home in a basket. Plan the dinner around what you found. Fresh bread, vegetables, cheese and fruit make a Roman supper.
practices.why: Roman markets overflowed with fresh produce, and shopping for the evening meal was part of daily life. Choosing by season brings a similar pleasure.
variations: Try a food you have never cooked.

practices.name: Dinner in company
practices.instructions: Eat the main meal of the day early, after bathing, and never alone if you can help it. Serve it in three stages: something small to open, eggs, olives, salad; then the main dishes; then fruit and nuts. Take off your shoes and lean back if you like. Talk, tell stories and listen. The rule of this Onda is never to dine alone.
practices.why: The Roman cena was the social centre of the day, a meal with several courses among friends. Eating in company, in stages, slows the evening in a good way.
variations: Lay the table with a cloth and a lamp.

practices.name: Write a letter
practices.instructions: Before bed write a proper letter to a friend who is away. Begin with a greeting and end with a farewell. Tell them what you have done and seen, give your opinion on some matter of the day, ask after their health and their family. Send it by post if you can. Pliny the Younger and Cicero wrote hundreds, and we read them still.
practices.why: Letters were how Romans kept friendships alive across a great empire. Writing a good one is a lost art.
variations: Ask a question and wait for the answer.

practices.name: Tell of an ancestor
practices.instructions: At the table or by the lamp, tell a story about one of your ancestors or an older relative: what they did, what they were like, a saying of theirs. Roman families kept wax masks of ancestors in the hall and recited their deeds at funerals. Keep your family’s memory alive by telling it to someone younger. Write a line to remember.
practices.why: Roman nobles displayed the masks of their ancestors and honoured them. Telling an ancestor’s story is the modern equivalent.
variations: Record an older relative telling a story.

practices.name: Read Virgil aloud
practices.instructions: Read a passage of the Aeneid aloud, such as the opening, the fall of Troy or Aeneas meeting Dido. Choose Fagles’s or another good translation and read with feeling. Romans read poetry aloud, not silently. Notice the rhythm. Stop at a good place and sit a moment.
practices.why: Virgil’s Aeneid was the national epic of Rome. Reading aloud brings out its music, which Romans valued above all.

practices.name: A game of latrunculi
practices.instructions: Play latrunculi, the Roman strategy game of capturing by sandwiching, with a friend. Draw a grid on paper and use coins or pebbles in two colours. Capture a piece by trapping it between two of yours. The rules are partly lost, so agree your own. Play two games and shake hands.
practices.why: Ludus latrunculorum, the game of little soldiers, was a favourite of Roman soldiers and gentlemen. Part of the pleasure is making your own rules.

practices.name: A recitation
practices.instructions: Choose a poem you love and recite it aloud to a friend or the room, from memory if you can. Romans held recitationes, poetry readings, in houses and halls. Stand up, project your voice and pause at the line ends. If you have no poem, read one by Catullus, Horace or Ovid. Receive applause graciously.
practices.why: Public recitals were a feature of Roman cultural life. Reading or reciting aloud makes poems come alive.
variations: Learn a short poem by heart.
Hold a small reading with friends.

practices.name: A day at the baths
practices.instructions: Spend an afternoon as a Roman at the baths: go to a public pool, spa or sauna with a friend, exercise first, then bathe in stages, from warm to hot to cool. Rest, talk and have a light snack. Take a book. Read the safety signs, drink water and leave if you feel unwell. Emerge clean and relaxed.
practices.why: The baths were the great social institution of Rome, with exercise, bathing, reading and conversation under one roof. An afternoon in the same spirit is a gift.
variations: Finish with a cold plunge if safe.

practices.name: A Saturnalia
practices.instructions: Hold a Saturnalia, the Roman midwinter festival of reversal and gifts. Draw lots for a king of the party, swap places so the youngest gives the orders, and exchange small, silly presents. Serve a good meal, play games and sing. Greet everyone with io Saturnalia. Keep it light-hearted and kind, and let everyone laugh.
practices.why: Saturnalia was the most loved Roman holiday: gifts, games, role reversal and feasting. It is a model for the spirit of Christmas and carnival.
variations: Make it a gift swap with a price limit.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of SPQR
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Mary Beard’s lively history of Rome. Pick one thing you did not know.

immersePlan.name: Read a letter of Pliny
immersePlan.text: Read a letter of Pliny the Younger, such as the one describing the eruption of Vesuvius, or one about his country house. Notice his tone.

immersePlan.name: Read a book of the Aeneid
immersePlan.text: Read Book 2 or Book 4 of Virgil’s epic aloud in Fagles’s translation. Notice how the story moves.

immersePlan.name: Watch Meet the Romans
immersePlan.text: Watch an episode of Mary Beard’s BBC series on the lives of ordinary Romans, from Pompeii to the poor. Listen for the surprises.

immersePlan.name: Watch an episode of I, Claudius
immersePlan.text: Watch an episode of the 1976 BBC drama of the emperors seen through the eyes of Claudius. Notice the acting and the intrigue.

immersePlan.name: Watch an episode of Rome
immersePlan.text: Watch the first episode of the HBO and BBC drama of Rome in the age of Caesar, seen from the streets. Note the details of daily life.

immersePlan.name: Listen to The History of Rome
immersePlan.text: Play an episode of Mike Duncan’s podcast, which tells the story from Aeneas to the last emperor. Listen while you walk.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the Pines of Rome
immersePlan.text: Play Respighi’s 1924 orchestral picture of Rome, from the games of children to the Appian Way at dawn. Imagine the scenes.

immersePlan.name: Hear music from ancient Rome
immersePlan.text: Play a recording of reconstructed Roman music on pipes, lyres and horns. Notice how different it sounds.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Augustus of Prima Porta
immersePlan.text: Look at the statue of the first emperor, standing in armour with his arm raised. Look at the small figures on his breastplate.

immersePlan.name: Look at Livia’s garden room
immersePlan.text: Look at the wall paintings of an imaginary garden, with trees, flowers and birds, from the villa of Livia. Count the birds.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Fayum portraits
immersePlan.text: Look at the painted faces of ordinary people from Roman Egypt, made to cover their mummies. Choose one person and imagine them.

immersePlan.name: Cook puls
immersePlan.text: Boil spelt, emmer or oats to a thick porridge and eat with a little oil and salt. It was the daily food of early Rome.

immersePlan.name: Make moretum
immersePlan.text: Pound garlic, hard cheese and herbs with a little oil and vinegar into a paste, and spread it on bread. It is the subject of a poem attributed to Virgil.

immersePlan.name: Bake libum
immersePlan.text: Mix fresh cheese with flour and an egg, shape into small cakes, bake and drizzle with honey. It was an offering cake, from Cato’s recipe.

immersePlan.name: Drink diluted grape juice
immersePlan.text: Mix grape juice with water in a jug and serve it in cups, as the Romans mixed wine. Use juice rather than wine.

immersePlan.name: Make mulsum without the wine
immersePlan.text: Stir honey into warm grape juice or warm water with a pinch of pepper. It is the Roman aperitif, without the alcohol.

immersePlan.name: Make posca
immersePlan.text: Mix water with a splash of vinegar and perhaps a little honey. It was the cheap, refreshing drink of soldiers and workers. Sip it cold.

immersePlan.name: Do a favour for someone who helped you
immersePlan.text: Think of someone who has helped you, and do something for them today, as a client served a patron. Say thank you out loud.

immersePlan.name: Recline at the table
immersePlan.text: Lay cushions on a couch or floor and eat a meal reclining on one elbow, as Romans did. Notice how it slows you down.

immersePlan.name: Tell a story of an ancestor
immersePlan.text: Tell a story about an ancestor to someone, as the Romans recited the deeds of their ancestors. Write a line to remember.

immersePlan.name: Play latrunculi
immersePlan.text: Play the Roman strategy game on a grid with two sets of pebbles. Trap pieces between two of yours.

immersePlan.name: Play tali and tesserae
immersePlan.text: Throw knucklebones or dice with a friend, as Romans did in the streets and taverns. Agree a small, silly stake.

immersePlan.name: Play harpastum
immersePlan.text: Play a gentle version of the Roman ball game: two teams, a small ball, passing to score. Play on grass and keep it friendly.

immersePlan.name: Mark Saturnalia
immersePlan.text: Saturnalia ran from 17 to 23 December. Give a small gift, swap roles with someone for an hour and say io Saturnalia.

immersePlan.name: Mark the Birthday of Rome
immersePlan.text: Rome’s traditional birthday is 21 April, the festival of Parilia. Make a toast to your city or town and share a meal.

immersePlan.name: Look up the Pantheon
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the Pantheon in Rome, its dome with the open eye at the top. Imagine the light moving across the floor.

immersePlan.name: Practise pietas
immersePlan.text: Pietas is duty to family, gods and country. Do one duty to your family today with a full heart.

immersePlan.name: Practise fides
immersePlan.text: Fides is good faith. Keep one promise to the letter today, even a small or inconvenient one, and note how it feels.

immersePlan.name: Practise otium
immersePlan.text: Otium is leisure, time to think and read. Spend half an hour on something you do for love, not for work.

rules.why: Begin each day by remembering where you come from and who depends on you.

rules.text: Business in the morning, leisure after
rules.why: Do your duties before noon. Do not mix the two.
Your word is your bond. A promise made is a debt, to friend or enemy.
A sound mind needs a sound body. Make time for both in the afternoon.
Share your main meal. A table is where friendship and good sense are kept up.
No haste, no complaint, no display of temper in public.

read.title: SPQR: A History of Ancient Rome
read.creator: Mary Beard
read.why: The best single book: a thousand years, told with attention to ordinary people and to how little we can be sure of.

read.title: The Letters of the Younger Pliny
read.creator: Pliny the Younger, trans. Betty Radice
read.why: A wealthy senator on his villas, his dinner parties, his uncle’s death under Vesuvius and what to do about the Christians.

read.title: The Aeneid
read.creator: Virgil, trans. Robert Fagles or Sarah Ruden
read.why: Rome’s national epic: a refugee from Troy founds a people at great cost. Written for Augustus, and more troubled than he may have noticed.

read.title: The Twelve Caesars
read.creator: Suetonius, trans. Robert Graves
read.why: Lives of the rulers from Julius Caesar to Domitian by a palace secretary with access to the archives and a taste for scandal.

read.title: The Satyricon
read.creator: Petronius
read.why: What survives of a comic novel. The dinner of the freed slave Trimalchio is the fullest picture of a Roman meal, exaggerated in every direction.

read.title: Memoirs of Hadrian
read.creator: Marguerite Yourcenar
read.why: A novel in the form of a letter from the dying emperor to the young Marcus Aurelius. Deeply researched and very beautiful.

watch.title: I, Claudius
watch.creator: BBC; Herbert Wise, from the novels of Robert Graves
watch.why: The first imperial family as a household drama of thirteen episodes, with Derek Jacobi as the stammering survivor.

watch.title: Meet the Romans with Mary Beard
watch.creator: BBC
watch.why: Three films about ordinary people of the city, read from their tombstones: bakers, slaves, children and wives.

watch.title: Rome
watch.creator: HBO and BBC
watch.why: The fall of the Republic seen from the street by two soldiers. The sets and the sense of a dirty, crowded, painted city are the best on film.

watch.title: Gladiator
watch.creator: Ridley Scott
watch.why: The history is loose, but the arena, the crowd and the idea of Rome as a dream worth dying for are all there.

listen.title: The History of Rome
listen.creator: Mike Duncan
listen.why: A podcast of 179 short episodes from the founding to 476. Clear, dry and addictive.

listen.title: Pines of Rome
listen.creator: Ottorino Respighi
listen.why: Four orchestral pictures. The last is a legion marching up the Appian Way at dawn.

listen.title: Music from Ancient Rome
listen.creator: Synaulia
listen.why: Reconstructions on copies of Roman instruments: reed pipes, lyre, water organ and frame drums.

listen.title: The Roman Empire
listen.creator: In Our Time, BBC Radio 4
listen.why: Dozens of forty-minute discussions on single subjects, from Hadrian’s Wall to the Augustan age.

art.title: Augustus of Prima Porta
art.creator: Roman sculptors
art.year: about 20 BCE, in a copy of the 1st century CE
art.why: The first emperor as a calm young general, barefoot like a god, his breastplate carved with a diplomatic victory. In the Vatican Museums.

art.title: The garden room of Livia
art.creator: Painters at the villa of Prima Porta
art.why: Four walls of a sunken dining room painted as a garden full of birds and fruit trees. In the Palazzo Massimo, Rome.

art.title: Trajan’s Column
art.creator: Attributed to Apollodorus of Damascus
art.why: A marble shaft thirty metres high with the story of two wars carved in a spiral of 2,600 figures. Still standing where it was put.

art.title: Mummy portraits from the Fayum
art.creator: Painters of Roman Egypt
art.why: Faces painted in wax on wood, placed over the dead. They look straight at you. The nearest we come to meeting the people of the empire.

eat.title: Puls
eat.creator: Emmer or spelt boiled to a porridge with salt, sometimes with cheese or beans
eat.why: The original food of the Romans, eaten long before bread, and always the food of the poor and the legions.

eat.title: Moretum
eat.creator: Garlic, hard cheese, coriander, rue, oil and vinegar pounded in a mortar
eat.why: A poem once credited to Virgil describes a farmer making it for his breakfast before dawn.

eat.title: Libum
eat.creator: A small cake of fresh cheese, flour and egg baked on bay leaves
eat.why: From Cato’s farming handbook of about 160 BCE. Offered to the household gods, and eaten warm with honey.

eat.title: Something with fish sauce
eat.creator: Lentils, greens or eggs seasoned with a few drops
eat.why: Garum, made from fermented fish, went into almost everything. The Italian anchovy sauce colatura is its descendant.

drink.title: Wine and water
drink.creator: Mixed in the cup, usually more water than wine
drink.why: Drunk by everyone at every meal. Only barbarians took it neat.

drink.title: Mulsum
drink.creator: Wine sweetened with honey
drink.why: Served cool with the first course of a dinner.

drink.title: Posca
drink.creator: Water sharpened with sour wine or vinegar
drink.why: The drink of soldiers and workmen. Safe, cheap and refreshing.

customs.title: Patron and client
customs.creator: A ladder of obligation
customs.why: Almost every free person had someone above them to call on and someone below to help. Favours were remembered and repaid.

customs.title: The toga
customs.creator: Citizen’s dress
customs.why: Worn for the forum, the courts and the games. A boy put on the plain white toga of manhood at about fifteen, in a family ceremony.

customs.title: Reclining at table
customs.creator: Three couches, nine guests
customs.why: Diners lay on the left elbow and ate with the right hand. Children and, at first, women sat.

customs.title: The masks of the ancestors
customs.creator: Wax portraits in the hall
customs.why: Noble families kept likenesses of their office-holding forebears, and actors wore them in funeral processions so that the dead walked with the living.

games.title: Ludus latrunculorum
games.creator: Board game · Rome
games.why: The game of little soldiers: pieces on a grid capture by trapping an enemy between two of their own. Boards are found in forts across the empire.

games.title: Tali and tesserae
games.creator: Knucklebones and dice
games.why: Four knucklebones were thrown together, and the best throw, all different, was the Venus. Augustus played for small stakes and wrote to his family about his winnings.

games.title: Terni lapilli
games.creator: Board game · Rome
games.why: Three pebbles each on a small wheel or square: get three in a row. Hundreds of boards are scratched into the steps of public buildings.

games.title: Harpastum
games.creator: Ball game · Rome
games.why: A rough game with a small hard ball, snatched and passed between two sides. Played in the exercise yard before bathing.

festivals.title: Saturnalia
festivals.creator: 17 to 23 December
festivals.why: The best of days, the poet Catullus called it. Work stopped, masters served their slaves at table, everyone wore the cap of freedom and gave small presents and candles.

festivals.title: The Birthday of Rome
festivals.creator: 21 April
festivals.why: The Parilia, an old shepherds’ festival, was held to be the day Romulus founded the city. Rome still marks it with a costumed procession and fireworks.

festivals.title: Parentalia
festivals.creator: 13 to 21 February
festivals.why: Nine days for the family dead. Temples closed, and people carried wine, bread and violets to the tombs outside the walls.

festivals.title: Floralia
festivals.creator: 28 April to 3 May
festivals.why: The festival of Flora, goddess of blossom, with bright clothes, theatre and a good deal of licence.

places.title: The Roman Forum and the Palatine
places.creator: Rome, Italy
places.why: The centre of the Roman world. Walk the Sacred Way from the Arch of Titus to the Senate House, then climb to the emperors’ palaces.

places.title: The Pantheon
places.creator: Piazza della Rotonda, Rome, Italy
places.why: Hadrian’s temple to all the gods, in use for nineteen centuries. Its concrete dome, open to the sky, has never been surpassed in its kind.

places.title: Pompeii and Herculaneum
places.creator: Bay of Naples, Italy
places.why: Two towns stopped on a day in 79 CE, with their bars, bakeries, election notices and household shrines. Herculaneum is smaller and better preserved.

places.title: Ostia Antica
places.creator: Near Rome, Italy
places.why: The port of Rome, abandoned and silted over. Streets of apartment blocks, warehouses, baths and a theatre, with few visitors.

places.title: Hadrian’s Wall and Vindolanda
places.creator: Northumberland, United Kingdom
places.why: The north-west frontier. The fort at Vindolanda shows the wooden letters found there, including a birthday invitation from one officer’s wife to another.

places.title: The Baths of Caracalla
places.creator: Rome, Italy
places.why: The brick shell of a bathhouse for sixteen hundred people, opened in 216. Stand in the hot room and look up.

ethics.title: Pietas
ethics.text: Duty to gods, parents, family and country, in that widening order.
ethics.practice: Do one thing today for a parent or an elder, unasked.

ethics.title: Fides
ethics.text: Trustworthiness. Do what you said you would, and stand by those under your protection.
ethics.practice: Keep one promise today that it would be easy to let slide.

ethics.title: Gravitas
ethics.text: Take serious things seriously and carry responsibility without fuss.
ethics.practice: Hold back one flippant remark today, and one complaint.

ethics.title: Industria
ethics.text: Hard, steady work. Idleness was a vice. Leisure was to be earned.
ethics.practice: Finish the day’s main task before you allow yourself any amusement.

ethics.title: Clementia
ethics.text: Mercy from a position of strength. To spare the defeated was the mark of the great.
ethics.practice: Let someone off who is in your power.

ethics.title: Frugalitas
ethics.text: Plain living. The heroes of early Rome were farmers who went back to the plough.
ethics.practice: Eat one meal today that a Roman farmer would have recognised.

philosophy.title: Not for ourselves alone
philosophy.text: Cicero held that our country, our friends and humankind each have a claim on us. A private life with no public service is incomplete.
philosophy.practice: What do you give to the place you live in?

philosophy.title: The way of the ancestors
philosophy.text: Romans looked back for their standards. What had been tried and handed down carried more weight than a new argument.
philosophy.practice: Name one thing you do because your grandparents did. Is it wise?

philosophy.title: Otium and negotium
philosophy.text: A good life has both. Business gives leisure its dignity, and leisure gives business its purpose.
philosophy.practice: Is your free time restoring you, or only filling the hours?

philosophy.title: Peace and its price
philosophy.text: The Roman peace was real, and it was won by conquest and kept by force. Tacitus let a defeated chief say so.
philosophy.practice: Whose labour and whose defeat does your own security rest on?

philosophy.title: Citizenship
philosophy.text: Rome’s peculiar strength was that it made citizens of the conquered and of freed slaves. Belonging was by law and not by blood.
philosophy.practice: Who around you is treated as an outsider who could be let in?

philosophy.title: Law
philosophy.text: Rome’s most lasting creation. Disputes were to be settled by rules, argued in the open, the same for patron and client.
philosophy.practice: Is there a quarrel in your life that needs a rule more than a victory?

philosophy.title: Fame and memory
philosophy.text: Romans lived for the judgment of those who would come after. They carved their careers in stone.
philosophy.practice: What would your epitaph say if it listed only what you did for others?

philosophy.title: Captive Greece
philosophy.text: The conquerors went to school with the conquered. Roman culture is a borrowing made into something of its own.
philosophy.practice: What have you taken from people you thought beneath you?

intro: At its height in the second century the Roman Empire held perhaps sixty million people, about a fifth of everyone then alive. It ran from the hills of northern Britain to the cataracts of the Nile and from the Atlantic to the Euphrates, and for some two hundred years the whole of that space was at peace with itself, under one law, two shared languages and a single coinage. A merchant could travel from York to Alexandria on paved roads and protected seas without crossing a frontier. Nothing like it had existed in the West before, and nothing has since.

It began with a city. Rome was a small town on the Tiber that, over five centuries as a republic, conquered Italy and then the Mediterranean. The wealth and armies of that conquest destroyed the republic in a century of civil wars, which ended when Julius Caesar’s adopted heir defeated his last rivals in 31 BCE. He took the name Augustus and, while preserving the Senate, the elections and the language of liberty, quietly gathered all real power to himself. The system he devised lasted, with adjustments, for three hundred years.

What held the empire together was not mainly force. There were only about thirty legions for the whole of it. It was held by the cities, several thousand of them, each governed by its own local worthies, who competed to build baths, theatres and aqueducts and were rewarded with Roman citizenship. Rome was unusually generous with that status. Freed slaves became citizens, and their sons could hold office. By 212 every free inhabitant of the empire was a Roman. Spaniards, Africans and Syrians became emperors.

The life of a Roman of the towns followed a pattern that would be recognisable from one end of the empire to the other. One rose at dawn, made an offering at the household shrine and attended to business: clients called on patrons, the courts sat, the markets opened. Work stopped around midday. The afternoon belonged to the baths, the great social institution of the Roman world, where one exercised, sweated, washed and talked. Dinner followed, in company. The virtues admired were those of duty: pietas towards family and gods, fides in keeping one’s word, gravitas in bearing.

This order rested on things we find hard to look at. Perhaps one person in six across the empire was a slave, and in Italy more. Conquest was brutal, and the amusements of the arena were killings. Women were under legal guardianship, though many ran businesses and estates. Romans themselves wrote about these things with surprising frankness.

The western empire broke up in the fifth century under the pressure of migrating peoples, plague and its own divisions. The eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, continued for another thousand years. Roman law, the Latin alphabet, the calendar, the idea of citizenship and the memory of a universal peace remained. This Onda takes the shape of a Roman day: the shrine, the morning’s duty, the afternoon bath, the shared dinner and the letter by lamplight.
guide.origin: The city of Rome, and a world that reached from Scotland to the Euphrates
guide.era: Augustus became sole ruler in 27 BCE. The last western emperor was deposed in 476 CE. The eastern empire lasted until 1453

figures.name: Augustus
figures.bio: Born Gaius Octavius. The first emperor, who ruled for forty-one years and called himself only first citizen. Cold, patient and extraordinarily able.

figures.name: Livia Drusilla
figures.bio: His wife for fifty-two years and his closest adviser, mother of the next emperor. The first woman in Roman public life to hold lasting power.

figures.name: Cicero
figures.bio: Lawyer, consul and the greatest Latin prose writer, killed defending the Republic. His works on duty and friendship formed the Roman idea of a gentleman.

figures.name: Marcus Agrippa
figures.bio: The friend who won Augustus his battles, then built Rome’s aqueducts, sewers, first public baths and the first Pantheon.

figures.name: Virgil
figures.bio: A farmer’s son from near Mantua who wrote the Aeneid. He asked on his deathbed for it to be burned.

figures.name: Pliny the Younger
figures.bio: Lawyer, senator and governor, whose ten books of letters are the best picture of a decent upper-class Roman life.

figures.name: Trajan
figures.bio: Born in Spain, the first emperor from the provinces. Under him the empire reached its greatest extent. The Senate’s wish for later emperors was to be luckier than Augustus and better than Trajan.

figures.name: Hadrian
figures.bio: The travelling emperor, who visited nearly every province, fixed the frontiers, rebuilt the Pantheon and designed his own villa at Tivoli.

figures.name: Claudia Severa
figures.bio: Wife of a fort commander in northern Britain. Her invitation to a friend’s birthday party, with a greeting in her own hand, is the earliest known writing in Latin by a woman.

figures.name: Septimius Severus
figures.bio: Born at Leptis Magna in what is now Libya, of Punic and Italian descent. A soldier emperor who died at York.

figures.name: Constantine
figures.bio: He reunited the empire, gave legal standing to Christianity and founded a new capital on the Bosporus.

history.detail: Romulus marks out the city on the Palatine on 21 April, by the reckoning of the scholar Varro. Archaeology finds huts there from about that time.
The last king is expelled. Rome is governed by annual magistrates and the Senate for the next five centuries.
Three wars make Rome master of the western Mediterranean. Carthage and Corinth are both destroyed in 146.
Julius Caesar, dictator for life, is stabbed to death in the Senate. Thirteen more years of civil war follow.
Having defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium, Octavian restores the Republic in name and receives a new title from the Senate. The Principate begins.
Much of Rome burns for six days. Nero rebuilds with wider streets and a vast palace, and blames the Christians.
Pompeii and Herculaneum are buried in August or October of 79. The following year Titus opens the great amphitheatre with a hundred days of games.
Trajan dies having added Dacia, Arabia and briefly Mesopotamia. Hadrian gives up the last and builds walls.
A pandemic, probably smallpox, kills several million. Marcus Aurelius spends his reign fighting on the Danube.
The emperor Caracalla grants Roman citizenship to every free person in the empire.
Fifty years of invasion, plague, inflation and more than twenty emperors. Diocletian restores order and divides the administration.
Christianity is made lawful. Constantinople is dedicated as a second Rome.
Alaric’s Goths enter the city, the first foreign army to do so in eight hundred years.
The boy emperor Romulus Augustulus is pensioned off by a general named Odoacer. The eastern empire continues until 1453.

concepts.detail: Augustus held a bundle of traditional powers and was called princeps, first citizen. The Senate still met, and everyone understood where decisions were made.

concepts.text: A legal status open to outsiders.
concepts.detail: It carried the right to a Roman marriage, to make a will, to appeal to the emperor and to be spared flogging. Its steady extension is the secret of the empire’s endurance.
Personal ties of protection and service ran from the emperor down to the freed slave. Offices, loans, verdicts and dinner invitations all moved along them.
Developed by jurists case by case and codified under Justinian in the sixth century. It underlies the legal systems of most of Europe and Latin America.
Rome governed through self-administering towns. To be civilised was, literally, to live in one, with a forum, baths and a council.
People were enslaved by capture, birth or sale and had no legal personality. Freeing slaves was common, and the freed became citizens, which was unique to Rome.
Public cult was a matter of correct performance, not belief. Rome absorbed the gods of the conquered, and asked only that the emperor’s welfare be prayed for.
Some two hundred thousand citizens in Rome received free grain, and there were more than a hundred days of public shows a year. The phrase is a satirist’s sneer.
Provincials adopted Latin or Greek, the toga, the bathhouse and Roman names, largely by choice and for advantage, while keeping local gods and customs.

facts.text: The dome of the Pantheon is unreinforced concrete, forty-three metres across, and was the largest in the world for thirteen centuries.
The Romans built some eighty thousand kilometres of paved road.
By the fourth century the city of Rome had eleven great public baths and more than eight hundred smaller ones.
July and August are named after Julius Caesar and Augustus.
The Roman hour varied with the season, since daylight was always divided into twelve.
Among the graffiti of Pompeii is the complaint: wall, I wonder that you have not fallen down, since you bear the tedious scribblings of so many.

sensitivity.note: This Onda follows the day of a free citizen of a Roman town. That day was made possible by conquest and by the labour of enslaved people. The practices borrow the pattern and the virtues. They do not celebrate the empire.
requiredCaveats: Perhaps one in six people in the empire was enslaved. Baths were stoked, dinners cooked and letters carried by people with no choice in the matter.
The household offering is given here as a gesture of gratitude to those you come from. Adapt it to your own belief or leave out the offering.
Roman public life excluded women from office and placed them under guardianship, and the games of the arena were public killings.
